question.text:
A 68-year-old right-handed male is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of sudden-onset weakness. He woke up with clumsiness in his left hand, which quickly progressed to weakness on his left side, more pronounced in the arm than the leg. His medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia, but he has not refilled his medications in a year. He has a 40-year history of smoking one pack of cigarettes daily. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse of 98/min, respirations of 20/min, and blood pressure of 200/110 mm Hg. Physical examination shows slurred speech, left-sided facial weakness sparing the forehead, 2/5 strength in the left upper limb, and 4/5 strength in the left lower limb, with normal strength and sensation on the right side. MRI reveals a right-sided infarct in the paramedian pontine base. Which additional finding is most likely in this patient?
Answer Choices: (A) Ipsilateral tongue deviation (B) Contralateral loss of proprioception (C) Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face (D) Eye deviation to the left (E) Vertical gaze palsy (F) Ipsilateral facial weakness involving the forehead (G) Eye deviation to the right (H) Loss of pupillary light reflex on the right (I) Bitemporal hemianopia (J) Contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing

options.F: Ipsilateral facial weakness involving the forehead
options.H: Loss of pupillary light reflex on the right

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with left-sided weakness and slurred speech, indicating a right hemisphere lesion. The MRI shows a right-sided infarct in the paramedian pontine base, which is consistent with a pontine stroke. The pontine region controls eye movements, facial muscles, and upper limb strength. Ipsilateral tongue deviation (A) is a classic sign of pontine involvement because the pontine nuclei control tongue movement, and damage to the right pontine base would affect the right side of the tongue. The other options are less specific to this type of lesion: contralateral hemiparesis (B) would suggest a more cortical lesion, and vertical gaze palsy (E) is more associated with lesions in the midbrain or brainstem tegmentum.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: MRI revealing a right-sided infarct in the paramedian pontine base
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Cortical infarct, cerebellar infarct, or midbrain lesion were considered but ruled out by the MRI location. The pontine infarct is the most specific diagnosis, leading to ipsilateral facial and tongue weakness.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has a right paramedian pontine infarct, which typically affects cranial nerve nuclei and pathways. The classic presentation includes ipsilateral facial weakness (including forehead) and contralateral hemiparesis, but in pontine strokes, eye deviation (ipsilateral to the lesion) is a hallmark due to disruption of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and abducens nerve pathways. The patient’s left-sided weakness and facial droop (spared forehead) suggest a right pontine lesion, and eye deviation to the left (ipsilateral to lesion) is expected. Other options like vertical gaze palsy or pupillary reflex loss are less specific and not typical of paramedian pontine infarcts.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Right paramedian pontine infarct with left hemiparesis and left facial weakness (spared forehead) strongly suggests involvement of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and abducens nucleus, leading to ipsilateral eye deviation (left eye deviation).
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: We considered other stroke locations (e.g., middle cerebral artery, basilar artery) but the MRI localization to the paramedian pons and the specific pattern of weakness (facial sparing of forehead, eye deviation) point to pontine syndrome. Other options like vertical gaze palsy or pupillary loss are more associated with midbrain or hypothalamic lesions.
